newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa sees healthy investment, trade - minister.
newsitem.headline: South Africa sees healthy investment, trade - minister.

text.p: Foreign investment in South Africa is growing at a healthy rate and is one of the key forces contributing to the country's economic growth, Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin said.
Erwin told Reuters that investment was increasing and was spread across the economy, unlike in the 1980s and early 1990s.
"The level of investment in South Africa is growing at a very healthy rate.
"It is one of the key driving forces in the growth process at present and we are very pleased with that," Erwin said in an interview late on Tuesday.

Inward investment jumped to 3.7 billion rand in 1995 from 821 million in 1994."Investment performance at the moment is very healthy. I don't have the exact figures but if we look at direct long-term investment, then we are very satisfied with what is happening," he added.
Erwin said companies which disinvested from South Africa under apartheid had now reinvested -- an important sign of confidence.
"What we are starting to see, too, is new investors -- Malaysia, Korea and one or two Indian investors coming in. These are new investors and that is another healthy sign," he added.

He said all projections indicated an extremely buoyant investment climate. "In fact I think many people underestimate the investment prospects, epecially because they are linked to our really good performance on the trade front.
"And our trade expansion with Africa, Asia and Latin America is a very healthy performance, showing we are clearly turning the corner on competitiveness," Erwin said.
But he said South Africa's relatively high interest rates remained a hurdle for investors, as did the unstable rand, which lost 29 percent of its value against the dollar last year.
Erwin was upbeat about opportunities for trade. "I think the trade opportunities are absolutely staggering".

"The African market is proving to be an exciting market for South Africa and the opening for South Africa of new markets in Asia, Latin America and the Middle East means that the opportunities are vastly greater than anything we have had before," Erwin said.
He added that South Africa would host numerous trade delegations in 1997, focusing on traditional trading partners but also new markets in Asia and Latin America.
"There can't be a more exciting time in South Africa's trading history than now and anyone that is not seeing that -- well, they must just go out of business because they are really sleeping".
